answer:
1. The animation shows historical US data on whether buying a home beat renting over ten-year periods. Each door or house in the grid is a starting month. A lit one means the buyer was ahead after ten years, and a dark one means the renter was ahead. It uses FHFA home prices, BLS rents and Freddie Mac mortgage rates, and it is labeled "illustrative." A character named Nina stands for a renter who is asking whether her rent is wasted.

2. The view changes in three ways. The flat grid of squares tilts into a 3D street of houses stretching toward the horizon, with the dark stretch in the middle. A caption box appears with summary numbers. The scene then zooms in on Nina, who stands between an apartment building marked "rent" and a house, under the question "Is her rent money wasted?"

3. The text says that in most start months, about 3 in 4, the buyer was ahead after ten years. The renter-ahead stretch ran from April 2001 to December 2007. For holding periods of fifteen years, no start month in the record had the renter ahead. So buying historically won more often than not, but not always, and a ten-year horizon could still lose if you started at the wrong time. The footer says this is US-only history and not a forecast.

4. The animation gives no advice. The footer says "Not advice on whether to buy or rent." A viewer might come away thinking that how long you stay and when you buy matter a lot. Any further step, such as buying, would be the viewer's own inference.

5. The advice question has no answer from the animation. The picture and text only gave historical statistics and an explicit disclaimer. Any takeaway about the time horizon is my own reading, not something the animation said.
